transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-09
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Location: Zoom
Record: Yes
Attendees: Jared Miller (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Evan Park (Arbor - Head of ML), Rita Solano (Arbor - CTO), Marco Li (Arbor - Infra)

Summary:
High-level intake to understand Arbor's per-token cost sensitivity, batching/caching levers, and hosting preferences (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer is cost-constrained, targeting sub-$0.0009 per-token avg for high-volume assistants; evaluating tradeoffs vs latency. Action items and pilot scope agreed: Redwood to produce pilot pricing and run benchmark using Arbor's 8k prompt set.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and volume profile
- Success criteria and budget constraints
- Latency targets and 95th percentile SLOs
- Batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization levers
- Hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment tradeoffs
- Security concerns (KMS, VPC, SOC 2)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jared (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Jared, AE on the infra team. Priya is our SE who will dig into perf. Evan, do you want to kick off with where you are and why we pulled this call together?
[00:22] Evan (Arbor): Yeah sure, thanks Jared. We're building a customer-facing assistant that handles conversational QA and doc retrieval. Volume's still ramping but we're planning for a big Q3 push. Primary question: can Redwood get us under our target token cost without killing latency. We're currently ~1.2M tokens/day in staging, expect 5–8M in production.
[00:45] Rita (CTO): And just to add, security and data residency matter. We may need VPC-only for certain customers. Also curious what the SLA looks like if we go dedicated.
[01:05] Priya (Redwood SE): Got it. Quick clarifying q: what's the typical prompt length and response length? That drives batching.
[01:15] Marco (Infra): Typical prompt is 400–700 tokens, responses avg 250 tokens, but we have longer summarization flows up to 3k tokens occasionally.
[01:30] Priya: Okay that distribution helps a lot — batching gains differ for 700/250 vs 3k sequences. Also are you doing streaming or full-response bulk?
[01:45] Evan: We stream for UX, but can accept small added latency if it reduces cost. 95th pct latency target is ~400ms end-to-end for short queries.
[02:02] Jared: Cool. On pricing goals you said sub-$0.0009 per token average? Can you share more on what that includes — embedding/recall tokens or strictly completion tokens?
[02:17] Evan: It's a blended target across prompt+completion tokens per user interaction — arithmetic average. We're ok with variance but want predictable monthly burn.
[02:30] Priya: Two levers we'll look at: batching (reduces per-token compute by increasing GPU utilization) and KV/prefix caching (saves repeated prefix tokens). On Redwood hosted we can apply continuous batching and auto-prefix cache; dedicated gives stronger isolation and can lower cost per token in steady throughput.
[02:55] Rita: What's the ballpark delta between hosted and dedicated? Like percent cost savings realistic?
[03:05] Priya: It varies with steady state QPS and variance. For stable workloads with good batching, dedicated can be 10–30% cheaper per-token excluding committed discounts. On hosted, you pay elasticity which helps for variable spikes. Also quantization and model selection (smaller compatible model) can reduce costs.
[03:30] Marco: When you say batching gains, is that just throughput improvement or does it change token billing? We bill tokens to customers, but our cloud spend is compute. Need to map token-per-dollar.
[03:45] Jared: Right — Redwood pricing is per-token for hosted; for dedicated it's a capacity/reservation pricing model plus optionally per-token for overage. The math gets interesting: e.g., with batching you might get 2–3x more throughput per GPU, so your effective $/token goes down. We can show a model.
[04:10] Evan: We want an example using our distribution. Can you run a benchmark with our set?
[04:18] Priya: Absolutely. If you share same prompt set & some traffic shape we'll run it in our staging to capture real batching efficiency and KV cache hit rates. That will feed into a blended per-token model.
[04:34] Rita: Also curious about KV cache — is that for recent conversation prefixes or full doc retrieval caching?
[04:44] Priya: Prefix/KV cache is mostly for autoregressive key-value caching (KV cache) which preserves previously computed keys across requests — very helpful for multi-turn. We also have an application-layer prefix cache to dedupe identical prompts. Cache hit rates are workloads dependent.
[05:05] Marco: Any details on TTLs or cache invalidation? Customers with sensitive PII require short TTLs.
[05:14] Priya: TTLs are configurable; we can support short TTLs for sensitive flows but that reduces savings. We'll show a sensitivity analysis.
[05:25] Jared: On the security side Rita — Redwood supports VPC connectors, KMS integration, and SOC 2. We can share our security pack. For Private/on-prem we also have an air-gapped option but that's a heavier lift.
[05:40] Rita: Good. For certain enterprise customers we will need HSM/KMS and audit logs.
[05:48] Jared: Noted.
[06:00] Evan: Back to cost — what about quantization? We've heard 4-bit quantized models reduce cost but might impact quality.
[06:08] Priya: Yes, quantization is another lever. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload. For many instruction-following tasks 4-bit often preserves quality, but you have to validate. We'll include a quality delta estimate in the bench.
[06:28] Marco: So what would the pilot look like? We want to compare hosted baseline vs dedicated reserved pool vs private minimal setup.
[06:36] Jared: Typical pilot: 2–3 week benchmarking window. Redwood runs hosted baseline tests on your prompt set, then a dedicated reserved node test (short reserved period or trial capacity), and we instrument KV cache and batching knobs to measure hit rates and token economics. We deliver a spreadsheet with blended $/token under each configuration plus latency percentiles.
[06:58] Evan: Does dedicated require longer-term commitment? 
[07:03] Jared: Dedicated has reserved capacity contracts typically monthly/annual. For pilots we can offer short-term trial capacity or discounted initial month to mimic reserved.
[07:14] Rita: How do fallbacks work? If dedicated pool is saturated, does Redwood route to hosted variants?
[07:23] Priya: Yes, smart routing and fallback policies exist — you can configure tiered fallbacks (dedicated -> hosted regional -> smaller model) to keep availability. That impacts cost predictability but preserves uptime.
[07:42] Marco: Any auto-scaling? We don't want to manage infra scaling ourselves in dedicated.
[07:48] Jared: Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling policies and burst capacity. You set SLOs and throughput targets; Redwood can autoscale within the reserved capacity plus burst margins if configured.
[08:02] Evan: We sell to Europe and US. Any residency constraints?
[08:09] Jared: Redwood has regions and Private deployments can be VPC-only in specific regions. We'll need to map your customer residency needs during the pilot.
[08:20] Rita: Ok. On pricing examples — can you give a quick sketch now just to see if we're in the same ballpark?
[08:27] Priya: Quick, rough example: Hosted generation $/token might be $0.0012 for current model at small scale; with prefix caching + batching we often see effective $/token go down to $0.00085–0.00095 depending on hit rates and batching. Dedicated steady-state after reserved discounts could reach $0.00065–0.0008. These are illustrative. We'll produce a tailored calc.
[08:55] Evan: That aligns with our target if we can get to mid-$0.0008s.
[09:02] Marco: When you say batching efficiency, is that measured as GPU tokens/sec uplift or end-to-end user latency impact?
[09:10] Priya: Both. We measure GPU tokens/sec and convert to $/token. We also show latency percentiles since larger batches can add micro-batching latency; continuous batching tries to balance latency by adaptive timers.
[09:28] Rita: Any specifics on model selection? Are there Redwood-verified smaller models that keep quality?
[09:35] Priya: Yes we have a model catalog with curated open models and verified perf profiles. We'll recommend model variants and quant profiles in the report.
[09:45] Evan: About cache hit rates — we currently have ~60% reuse on multi-turn chat for internal tests. If we get 60% KV hit, how much does that translate to cost savings?
[09:58] Priya: If your KV caching avoids recomputing large prefixes that are say 300 tokens on average, a 60% hit can reduce prompt tokens substantially. In rough terms, 50–60% hit with good batching could halve your prompt-related compute for those flows; overall savings depend on how much of your total token volume those multi-turn chats represent.
[10:22] Marco: Ok makes sense.
[10:30] Jared: I want to flag a few tradeoffs we should capture in the bench: privacy vs caching TTL, dedicated reservation vs elasticity, model size vs output quality. We'll document sensitivity curves.
[10:45] Evan: Great. A couple of procurement Qs — if we go dedicated who signs the infra SLA? Anything special?
[10:54] Jared: Typically Redwood signs an SLA tied to Dedicated. For enterprise deals we do a commercial SLA and support package. We'll include that in the pilot packet.
[11:05] Rita: Also OOTB integrations — SSO/SAML and RBAC?
[11:10] Jared: Yes SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC, audit logs — we'll include the security pack link.
[11:20] Evan: Can you show us the worksheet of how you modeled per-token math previously?
[11:25] Priya: We have a spreadsheet template; we'll populate with your prompts. Link note: pilot calc template will be shared (link: redwood.ai/pilot-template).
[11:40] Marco: Is streaming more expensive than non-streaming? Any delta?
[11:45] Priya: Streaming itself isn't a big compute delta; it's more about latency targets. There is some overhead for more frequent network frames but cost is dominated by model forward passes. If streaming forces smaller batch windows, you may lose batching efficiency which increases $/token.
[12:02] Evan: So small tradeoff: streaming latency vs $/token. Understood.
[12:10] Jared: Let's talk telemetry — we can instrument token-level cost, per-route latency, and per-token breakdowns. This will help you see which customers or flows are burning most tokens.
[12:23] Rita: We'll want token-level attribution in our console and export to our billing system.
[12:30] Jared: That's possible; Redwood Console supports token-level cost breakdown and route tagging.
[12:38] Evan: Any examples of companies that moved from hosted to dedicated and what percent savings they saw?
[12:45] Priya: Variation but we've seen clients with stable loads see 15–25% savings purely from reserved capacity and better packing. With aggressive quantization and high cache hit rates we saw cases approaching 40% overall savings. We'll anonymize case studies.
[13:05] Marco: On the pilot, what metrics will you capture?
[13:09] Priya: We'll capture tokens/sec per GPU, median and 95/99 latency, cache hit rates, per-route $/token, effective $/prompt and $/session, and model quality regression metrics on a few eval prompts.
[13:25] Evan: Good. For the quality metric how do you measure hallucination/regression?
[13:29] Priya: We'll use Redwood Optimize — automated evals on your labeled prompt set, plus human spot checks for sensitive flows. We'll report any degradation when applying quantization or model swaps.
[13:45] Rita: About private/on-prem — what's the operational lift? We have an internal SRE team but limited time.
[13:53] Jared: Private deployments require integration work (VPC peering, KMS/HSM setup). On-prem air-gapped is the highest lift. We provide a private control plane and operations runbook; many customers keep Redwood managed but behind their VPC. We'll scope effort in the pilot.
[14:10] Evan: Ok. Any red flags for us?
[14:14] Priya: Main risk is if your workload is too spiky with low batching opportunities; then hosted might be best for cost predictability but per-token cost may be higher. Also strict short TTLs reduce caching benefits.
[14:29] Marco: Noted.
[14:34] Rita: A legal Q — do you retain user data for model fine-tuning? We won't allow any customer data to be used for model training.
[14:42] Jared: Redwood does not use customer data to train models by default; we'll include that guarantee in enterprise contracts and SOC 2 docs.
[14:54] Evan: One more ops detail — do you provide per-route throttles so we can prioritize critical flows?
[15:01] Priya: Yes per-route rate limits and priority routing are supported. You can also set cost ceilings per route.
[15:12] Jared: Great. Sounds like we have a path: you share prompt set and QPS shape, we run hosted baseline and dedicated mimic and produce a calc + security pack.
[15:23] Evan: Timeline ok — we'll get you the data by next Monday.
[15:28] Jared: Perfect. We'll aim to return results within 7 business days after we have data.
[15:33] Priya: I'll set up the staging run once we receive the dataset; we may ask for a small sample of traffic logs to simulate spike patterns.
[15:40] Rita: Also include a short doc on cache TTL tradeoffs and suggested defaults.
[15:46] Jared: Will do.
[15:50] Evan: Anything else on cost levers we should know?
[15:53] Priya: A final note: routing by model family (cheaper variants for non-critical routes) is a big lever — split user flows so mission-critical queries use higher-quality model while batch analytics uses cheaper models. That usually preserves UX while saving cost.
[16:10] Marco: Ok that seems actionable.
[16:15] Jared: Quick recap of next steps: Jared sends pricing + contract + security pack, Priya runs bench and returns results, Evan provides prompt set and QPS, schedule review call.
[16:29] Evan: Sounds good. Appreciate it.
[16:33] Rita: Thanks everyone.
[16:36] Jared: Thanks — we'll follow up with calendar invite for benchmark review.
